opus-5.5.text:
I think it remains very useful, honestly, and in some ways factories are exactly the setting where task and motion planning shines. When you have a structured environment, where you know the objects, you know the geometry, you have good CAD models, and the state is largely observable, then the core assumptions behind TAMP actually hold. You can write down the symbolic abstractions, the preconditions and effects, and the planner can reason over long horizons with guarantees that a learned policy just can't give you right now.

And in manufacturing, those guarantees matter a lot. People care about reliability, about cycle time, about being able to verify and explain why the robot did what it did. If something fails on an assembly line, you want to be able to trace it back. A planning-based system gives you that interpretability and that compositionality: you can reconfigure the task, swap in a new part, and the planner figures out a new sequence without needing to collect a whole new dataset.

Where it struggles is when the world gets messy: deformable objects, cluttered bins, contact-rich insertion with tight tolerances, or situations where you can't easily model the dynamics. That's where learning has really pushed ahead. So the way I see it, the most promising direction isn't one versus the other. It's combining them: using learned models for perception, for low-level skills, maybe even for learning the abstractions themselves, and then using planning to stitch those skills together over long horizons. A lot of my own work has been in that space, trying to get the generalization of learning with the structure and reasoning of planning.

So in constrained settings like factories, I'd say TAMP is not going away. If anything, it's a strong backbone, and learning is what lets it extend to the parts of the problem that are hard to model by hand.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts TAMP with learned policies and says learning helps with harder-to-model factory tasks, but it does not say factory-system builders may choose less principled alternatives to TAMP.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it remains extremely useful, and honestly I'd push back a little on the framing that it's something we're waiting to move past. In a factory, you have a lot of the things that classical task and motion planning was designed around: the environment is mostly known, you can often get a good geometric model of the workcell, the set of objects is bounded, and the cost of a mistake is high. In that regime, TAMP gives you something that learning-based policies still struggle to give you, which is a guarantee. If the planner returns a trajectory, you know it satisfies the kinematic constraints, it avoids collisions in the model, and the sequence of actions is logically consistent with the goal. That kind of verifiability matters a lot when you're moving a heavy part next to a human operator or a million-dollar machine.

Where I think the interesting question lies is in the boundary. Pure TAMP assumes you can write down the symbolic abstractions and the geometric models by hand, and that assumption breaks the moment the factory gets a little messy. Parts come in slightly deformed, a bin is cluttered, a fixture shifts by a few millimeters, or the task involves contact-rich manipulation like insertion or cable routing where the physics is hard to model. That's exactly where learning has been making real progress. So the way I see it in practice is not "TAMP versus learning" but a division of labor. You let the planner handle the long-horizon structure, the sequencing, the hard constraints, and you let learned components handle perception, grasp prediction, and the low-level skills that are hard to specify analytically. A lot of my own work has been about making that interface less brittle, like learning the skill models or the feasibility predictors that a planner can then reason over.

The other thing I'd say is that factories are actually a great proving ground for this hybrid approach because you can iterate. You can collect data in the same cell for months, you can build digital twins, and you can afford to spend compute on planning. So rather than TAMP becoming obsolete in constrained settings, I think those settings are where it stays strongest the longest, and where we'll figure out how to blend it with learning before taking that recipe to more open-world environments like homes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning-based policies and hybrid TAMP systems, but does not say that factory-system builders may use less principled alternatives to TAMP.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s still very useful, especially in factories where you can structure the environment and define the task pretty precisely. You know the objects, you know the robot’s capabilities, and you have constraints you need to respect. That’s a setting where task and motion planning can work really well: deciding which operations to perform and finding motions that actually execute them.

The challenge is how much modeling and engineering you need to make that work. If something changes—an object is in an unexpected position, or a grasp fails—you need a way to recover. Learning can help with perception and those less predictable interactions, while planning provides structure. So I see a lot of value in combining them, particularly when reliability matters more than being able to handle every possible task.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the usefulness, engineering demands, and possible combination of planning with learning, but does not say factory-system builders may use less principled alternatives to task and motion planning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think task and motion planning is still very useful in those settings. In a factory, you can often specify the objects, the constraints, and what success looks like quite precisely. That structure gives a planner a lot to work with: it can reason about which operations need to happen, in what order, and whether the robot can physically execute them without collisions.

The challenge is that even a factory isn’t perfectly predictable. Parts can shift, perception can be uncertain, and a grasp can fail. So I see a strong role for combining planning with learned perception and control. The planner provides the structure, while the learned components help the robot handle variation and recover when execution doesn’t go as expected.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the value of planning and combining it with learned components, but does not say factory-system builders may choose less principled alternatives.
